claim: Constrained, cyclic peptides encoded by plant genes represent a new generation of drug leads.
source: Constrained, cyclic peptides encoded by plant genes represent a new generation of drug leads.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract presenting the significance of cyclic peptides as drug leads.

claim: Evolution has repeatedly recruited the Cys-protease asparaginyl endopeptidase (AEP) to perform head-to-tail ligation of cyclic peptides.
source: Evolution has repeatedly recruited the Cys-protease asparaginyl endopeptidase (AEP) to perform their head-to-tail ligation.
evidence: This statement is supported by the broader context of the manuscript discussing convergent evolution of AEPs for macrocyclization.

claim: AEP macrocyclization reactions use the substrate's amino terminus instead of water to deacylate, forming a peptide bond.
source: These macrocyclization reactions use the substrates amino terminus instead of water to deacylate, so a peptide bond is formed.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of macrocyclization as understood from the study.

claim: The crystal structure of an active plant AEP from Helianthus annuus was determined.
source: Here we present the crystal structure of an active plant AEP from the common sunflower, Helianthus annuus.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The active site of HaAEP1 contained electron density for a tetrahedral intermediate with partial occupancy.
source: The active site contained electron density for a tetrahedral intermediate with partial occupancy that predicted a binding mode for peptide macrocyclization.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure data.

claim: Substituting catalytic residues in HaAEP1 can alter the ratio of cyclic to acyclic products.
source: By substituting catalytic residues we could alter the ratio of cyclic to acyclic products.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutagenesis experiments and MALDI-MS analysis.

claim: AEPs from species lacking cyclic peptides can perform macrocyclization under favorable pH conditions.
source: Moreover, we showed AEPs from other species lacking cyclic peptides can perform macrocyclization under favorable pH conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally with AtAEP2 and RcAEP1.

claim: AEPs belong to the C13 family of cysteine proteases based on the presence of a His-Gly-spacer-Ala-Cys motif.
source: Asparaginyl endopeptidases (AEPs) are a group of asparagine/aspartic acid (Asx) specific proteases that have been classified as belonging to the C13 family of cysteine proteases based on the presence of a His-Gly-spacer-Ala-Cys motif (Hara-Nishimura et al., 1993; Chen et al., 1997; Mathieu et al., 2002; Shafee et al., 2015).
evidence: This classification is supported by multiple citations.

claim: AEPs were first described in plants as vacuolar processing enzymes based on their propensity for processing seed proteins stored in vacuoles.
source: First described in plants as vacuolar processing enzymes based on their propensity for processing seed proteins stored in vacuoles, AEPs have since been described in a variety of organisms and shown to be involved in a wide range of processes including, cell death antigen processing and hemoglobin degradation (Hara-Nishimura et al., 1993; Manoury et al., 1998; Hatsugai et al., 2004; Kuroyanagi et al., 2005; Yamada et al., 2005; Sojka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing AEP functions.

claim: AEPs are involved in cell death, antigen processing, and hemoglobin degradation.
source: First described in plants as vacuolar processing enzymes based on their propensity for processing seed proteins stored in vacuoles, AEPs have since been described in a variety of organisms and shown to be involved in a wide range of processes including, cell death antigen processing and hemoglobin degradation (Hara-Nishimura et al., 1993; Manoury et al., 1998; Hatsugai et al., 2004; Kuroyanagi et al., 2005; Yamada et al., 2005; Sojka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The ability of endoproteases to perform ligation reactions was first observed by Bergmann and Fruton in 1938 with chymotrypsin.
source: The ability of endoproteases to perform ligation reactions was first observed by Bergmann and Fruton in 1938 with chymotrypsin (Bergmann and Fruton, 1938).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: In vitro ligation reactions were performed with AEP from jack bean (Canavalia ensiformis) seeds.
source: Later, in vitro ligation reactions were performed with AEP from jack bean (Canavalia ensiformis) seeds (Bowles et al., 1986; Min and Jones, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Evolutionarily distinct plant families have repeatedly recruited AEPs to catalyze the formation of ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) through macrocyclization of linear precursor sequences.
source: The recent discovery that evolutionarily distinct plant families have repeatedly recruited AEPs to catalyze the formation of ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs), through the macrocyclization of linear precursor sequences, has caught the attention of drug designers keen to overcome the current inefficiencies in native chemical ligation that limit the therapeutic use of cyclic peptides (Pattabiraman and Bode, 2011; Mylne et al., 2012; Arnison et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Therapeutic cyclic peptides have the potential to capitalize on a niche in the pharmaceutical market by virtue of their intermediate size between small molecule drugs and large protein structures.
source: Such therapeutic cyclic peptides are viewed by many to have the potential to capitalize on a niche in the current pharmaceutical market by virtue of their intermediate size between small molecule drugs and large protein structures, and their unique capacity to combine favorable bioavailability and stability characteristics with high target specificity facilitated by tolerance to site-directed mutagenesis (Clark et al., 2005, 2010; Gould et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2013; Poth et al., 2013; Truman, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations discussing the properties of cyclic peptides.

claim: Cyclic peptides combine favorable bioavailability and stability characteristics with high target specificity facilitated by tolerance to site-directed mutagenesis.
source: Such therapeutic cyclic peptides are viewed by many to have the potential to capitalize on a niche in the current pharmaceutical market by virtue of their intermediate size between small molecule drugs and large protein structures, and their unique capacity to combine favorable bioavailability and stability characteristics with high target specificity facilitated by tolerance to site-directed mutagenesis (Clark et al., 2005, 2010; Gould et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2013; Poth et al., 2013; Truman, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Computational techniques for the discovery of RiPPs are improving.
source: Moreover, as computational techniques for the discovery of RiPPs improve and the number of cyclic peptides described continues to expand, an ever-wider array of scaffolds might be exploited to tailor molecules to specific drug targets (Bhardwaj et al., 2016; Truman, 2016; Hetrick and van der Donk, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The number of cyclic peptides described continues to expand.
source: Moreover, as computational techniques for the discovery of RiPPs improve and the number of cyclic peptides described continues to expand, an ever-wider array of scaffolds might be exploited to tailor molecules to specific drug targets (Bhardwaj et al., 2016; Truman, 2016; Hetrick and van der Donk, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: SFTI-1 is a 14-residue, bicyclic peptide with a cyclic backbone and an internal disulfide bond.
source: Sunflower trypsin inhibitor-1 (SFTI-1) is a 14-residue, bicyclic peptide with a cyclic backbone and an internal disulfide bond (Luckett et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: SFTI-1's sequence is buried within a precursor that also encodes seed storage albumin.
source: Its biosynthesis is rather unusual as its sequence is buried within a precursor that also encodes seed storage albumin.
evidence: This describes the unusual biosynthesis of SFTI-1.

claim: Seed storage albumins constitute over 50% of total seed protein.
source: Seed storage albumins are a major class of seed storage protein that constitute over 50% of total seed protein and become a source of nitrogen and sulfur during seed germination (Youle and Huang, 1978; Shewry and Halford, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Seed storage albumins become a source of nitrogen and sulfur during seed germination.
source: Seed storage albumins are a major class of seed storage protein that constitute over 50% of total seed protein and become a source of nitrogen and sulfur during seed germination (Youle and Huang, 1978; Shewry and Halford, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The common sunflower (Helianthus annuus) has many genes encoding precursors for napin-type or 2S seed storage albumins.
source: The common sunflower (Helianthus annuus) has many genes encoding precursors for these napin-type or 2S seed storage albumins that are synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum before undergoing cleavage maturation by AEP and localizing to storage vacuoles (Bollini and Chrispeels, 1979; Franke et al., 2016; Jayasena et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Napin-type or 2S seed storage albumins are synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum before undergoing cleavage maturation by AEP and localizing to storage vacuoles.
source: The common sunflower (Helianthus annuus) has many genes encoding precursors for these napin-type or 2S seed storage albumins that are synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum before undergoing cleavage maturation by AEP and localizing to storage vacuoles (Bollini and Chrispeels, 1979; Franke et al., 2016; Jayasena et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: SFTI-1 is post-translationally processed by AEP from within a unique seed storage albumin precursor called Preproalbumin with SFTI-1 (PawS1).
source: Along with an adjacent albumin, SFTI-1 is post-translationally processed by AEP from within a unique seed storage albumin precursor called Preproalbumin with SFTI-1 (PawS1) (Mylne et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: SFTI-1 is a potent inhibitor of serine proteases.
source: SFTI-1 is a potent inhibitor of serine proteases, and its intrinsic stability and cellular penetration capabilities have led to its application as a bioactive scaffold (White and Craik, 2016; Swedberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: SFTI-1's intrinsic stability and cellular penetration capabilities have led to its application as a bioactive scaffold.
source: SFTI-1 is a potent inhibitor of serine proteases, and its intrinsic stability and cellular penetration capabilities have led to its application as a bioactive scaffold (White and Craik, 2016; Swedberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: AEP-catalyzed macrocyclization of SFTI-1 is hypothesized to proceed via a cleavage-coupled intramolecular transpeptidation reaction.
source: AEP-catalyzed macrocyclization of SFTI-1 is hypothesized to proceed via a cleavage-coupled intramolecular transpeptidation reaction whereby catalysis begins with the deprotonation of the active site Cys by a localized His of the catalytic center, facilitating the nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl carbon of the Asp by the activated Cys thiol of AEP (Bernath-Levin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Catalysis begins with the deprotonation of the active site Cys by a localized His of the catalytic center.
source: AEP-catalyzed macrocyclization of SFTI-1 is hypothesized to proceed via a cleavage-coupled intramolecular transpeptidation reaction whereby catalysis begins with the deprotonation of the active site Cys by a localized His of the catalytic center, facilitating the nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl carbon of the Asp by the activated Cys thiol of AEP (Bernath-Levin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: The nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl carbon of the Asp by the activated Cys thiol of AEP culminates in the formation of a thioacyl intermediate between the substrate and AEP.
source: This attack culminates in the formation of a thioacyl intermediate between the substrate and AEP, and the removal of the C-terminus.
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic description.

claim: The reaction is concluded by the nucleophilic attack of the thioacyl intermediate by a Gly at the N-terminus of the substrate, resulting in the macrocyclization of SFTI-1 in a head-to-tail manner.
source: The reaction is proposed to be subsequently concluded by the nucleophilic attack of this intermediate by a Gly at the N-terminus of the substrate, resulting in the macrocyclization of SFTI-1 in a head-to-tail manner (Mylne et al., 2011; Bernath-Levin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic description supported by citations.

claim: The macrocyclization reaction proceeds in competition with nucleophilic attack upon the thioacyl intermediate by water molecules which would produce hydrolyzed, acyclic-SFTI.
source: Notably, this reaction proceeds in competition with nucleophilic attack upon the thioacyl intermediate by any nearby water molecules which would produce hydrolyzed, acyclic-SFTI.
evidence: This describes the competing reaction pathway.

claim: In vitro studies revealed the ratio of acyclic to cyclic SFTI-1 to be in the order of 5.8:1.
source: In vitro studies revealed the ratio of acyclic to cyclic SFTI-1 to be in the order of 5.8:1, with the less stable acyclic products hypothesized to be quickly degraded in vivo (Bernath-Levin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an experimental result supported by citation.

claim: The less stable acyclic products are hypothesized to be quickly degraded in vivo.
source: In vitro studies revealed the ratio of acyclic to cyclic SFTI-1 to be in the order of 5.8:1, with the less stable acyclic products hypothesized to be quickly degraded in vivo (Bernath-Levin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Evidence for AEP-mediated and hydrolysis-independent transpeptidation was demonstrated through the exclusion of a heavy atom O18 in the cyclic SFTI-1 product from an in vitro jack bean AEP (CeAEP1) catalyzed reaction.
source: Evidence for AEP-mediated and hydrolysis-independent transpeptidation was demonstrated through the exclusion of a heavy atom O18 in the cyclic SFTI-1 product from an in vitro jack bean AEP (CeAEP1) catalyzed reaction (Bernath-Levin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is experimental evidence supported by citation.

claim: The formation of a much larger cyclic peptide by an AEP from Oldenlandia affinis (OaAEP1) was shown to lack O18 incorporation, suggesting a conserved mechanism of macrocyclization despite differences in substrate sequences.
source: The formation of a much larger cyclic peptide by an AEP from Oldenlandia affinis (OaAEP1) was also shown to lack O18 incorporation, suggesting a conserved mechanism of macrocyclization despite differences in substrate sequences (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This is experimental evidence supported by citation.

claim: An AEP from butterfly pea (Clitoria ternatea) termed butelase one has been suggested to function only as a ligase.
source: However, the suggestion that an AEP from butterfly pea (Clitoria ternatea) termed butelase one functions only as a ligase (Nguyen et al., 2014), combined with the proposal of a succinimide-driven, cleavage-independent ligation event based on the crystal structure of human AEP (hAEP) and its ability to ligate substrate in the absence of the catalytic Cys, has cast uncertainty on the mechanism of AEP-catalyzed macrocyclization (Dall et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a suggestion from the literature supported by citation.

claim: A succinimide-driven, cleavage-independent ligation event has been proposed based on the crystal structure of human AEP (hAEP) and its ability to ligate substrate in the absence of the catalytic Cys.
source: However, the suggestion that an AEP from butterfly pea (Clitoria ternatea) termed butelase one functions only as a ligase (Nguyen et al., 2014), combined with the proposal of a succinimide-driven, cleavage-independent ligation event based on the crystal structure of human AEP (hAEP) and its ability to ligate substrate in the absence of the catalytic Cys, has cast uncertainty on the mechanism of AEP-catalyzed macrocyclization (Dall et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposal from the literature supported by citation.

claim: This is the first structure of an active plant AEP capable of performing peptide macrocyclization.
source: Herein, we describe the first structure of an active plant AEP; one capable of performing peptide macrocyclization.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: HaAEP1 is the most abundant AEP of five AEPs in the common sunflower.
source: This AEP, the most abundant AEP of five AEPs in the common sunflower (HaAEP1), displays structural similarity to previously published active AEPs from mammals, with subtle differences at residues involved in substrate recognition.
evidence: This is a statement about the identity of HaAEP1.

claim: HaAEP1 displays structural similarity to previously published active AEPs from mammals, with subtle differences at residues involved in substrate recognition.
source: This AEP, the most abundant AEP of five AEPs in the common sunflower (HaAEP1), displays structural similarity to previously published active AEPs from mammals, with subtle differences at residues involved in substrate recognition.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: AEPs are synthesized as inactive precursors that undergo irreversible auto-activation into their mature form on exposure to a low pH environment.
source: AEPs are synthesized as inactive precursors that have been shown to undergo irreversible auto-activation into their mature form on exposure to a low pH environment that resembles the acidic pH in the vesicles/vacuole where these proteins are active in vivo (Dall and Brandstetter, 2013; Shafee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The low pH environment for AEP activation resembles the acidic pH in the vesicles/vacuole where these proteins are active in vivo.
source: AEPs are synthesized as inactive precursors that have been shown to undergo irreversible auto-activation into their mature form on exposure to a low pH environment that resembles the acidic pH in the vesicles/vacuole where these proteins are active in vivo (Dall and Brandstetter, 2013; Shafee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: A ~51 kDa pro-HaAEP1 (residues 28–491) lacking an endoplasmic reticulum signal sequence and including a N-terminal His-tag was expressed in Escherichia coli.
source: In order to obtain an active form of a plant AEP, a ~51 kDa pro-HaAEP1 (residues 28–491) lacking an endoplasmic reticulum signal sequence and including a N-terminal His-tag was expressed in Escherichia coli and purified by nickel affinity chromatography before being activated at pH 4.0 overnight.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Pro-HaAEP1 was activated at pH 4.0 overnight.
source: In order to obtain an active form of a plant AEP, a ~51 kDa pro-HaAEP1 (residues 28–491) lacking an endoplasmic reticulum signal sequence and including a N-terminal His-tag was expressed in Escherichia coli and purified by nickel affinity chromatography before being activated at pH 4.0 overnight.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The activated form of HaAEP1 was purified by size exclusion chromatography, enabling separation of the core domain from the 'cap' domain.
source: The activated form of HaAEP1 was then further purified by size exclusion chromatography, enabling separation of the core domain from the 'cap' domain (Zhao et al., 2014), and crystal trials were undertaken (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: SDS-PAGE analysis of the ~38 kDa core domain peak revealed the disassociation of the core domain from the cap domain and showed several bands of HaAEP1, suggesting the presence of several cleavage sites at the termini of the core domain.
source: SDS-PAGE analysis of the ~38 kDa core domain peak revealed the disassociation of the core domain from the cap domain but also showed several bands of HaAEP1, suggesting the presence of several cleavage sites at the termini of the core domain, as seen previously for several AEPs (Hara-Nishimura et al., 1998; Nguyen et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2014; Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on SDS-PAGE analysis and supported by citations.

claim: Sequence comparison reveals the conservation of several predicted cleavage sites in HaAEP1 but notably lacks a previously described C-terminal di-Asp motif.
source: Indeed sequence comparison reveals the conservation of several of these predicted cleavage sites but notably lacks a previously described C-terminal di-Asp motif (Hiraiwa et al., 1999) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and supported by citation.

claim: Asp52, Asn57, Asn338, Asp356, and Asp358 might represent the dominant autocatalytic cleavage sites in HaAEP1.
source: This led us to hypothesize that Asp52, Asn57, Asn338, Asp356, and Asp358 might represent the dominant autocatalytic cleavage sites in HaAEP1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on sequence analysis.

claim: Crystallization trials of the ~38 kDa activated HaAEP1 yielded diffraction quality crystals that diffracted to a resolution of 1.8 Å.
source: Crystallization trials of the ~38 kDa activated HaAEP1 yielded diffraction quality crystals that diffracted to a resolution of 1.8 Å (Table 1).
evidence: This is crystallographic data.

claim: The crystal structure was solved by molecular replacement yielding a single monomer in the asymmetric unit.
source: The crystal structure was solved by molecular replacement yielding a single monomer in the asymmetric unit, and revealed an active monomeric HaAEP1 (residues 58–338 with weak electron density for Asn338) that forms a canonical C13 caspase structure, with a central six-stranded β-sheet region confined by five α-helices (Hara-Nishimura et al., 1993; Yamada et al., 2005) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the crystallographic results.

claim: HaAEP1 forms a canonical C13 caspase structure, with a central six-stranded β-sheet region confined by five α-helices.
source: The crystal structure was solved by molecular replacement yielding a single monomer in the asymmetric unit, and revealed an active monomeric HaAEP1 (residues 58–338 with weak electron density for Asn338) that forms a canonical C13 caspase structure, with a central six-stranded β-sheet region confined by five α-helices (Hara-Nishimura et al., 1993; Yamada et al., 2005) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the structure and is supported by citations.

claim: The structure of HaAEP1 lacks the C-terminal cap domain and N-terminal His-Tag.
source: The structure of HaAEP1 lacks the C-terminal cap domain and N-terminal His-Tag, displaying dimensions of approximately 44 Å x 42 Å x 39 Å.
evidence: This describes the structure.

claim: The structure of HaAEP1 displays dimensions of approximately 44 Å x 42 Å x 39 Å.
source: The structure of HaAEP1 lacks the C-terminal cap domain and N-terminal His-Tag, displaying dimensions of approximately 44 Å x 42 Å x 39 Å.
evidence: This describes the structure.

claim: The pro-domains are likely to have been auto-catalytically processed during maturation as the predicted Asn cleavage sites precede and follow the defined active structure.
source: Sequence analysis of this core domain suggests that the aforementioned pro-domains are likely to have been auto-catalytically processed during maturation as the previously predicted Asn cleavage sites precede and follow the defined active structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence analysis.

claim: HaAEP1 displays structural similarity to hAEP and OaAEP1 with an r.m.s.d. value of 1.0 and 0.7 Å over 262 and 267 carbon alpha residues, respectively.
source: HaAEP1 displays structural similarity to hAEP and a recently published structure of inactive OaAEP1 (PDB ID: 4N6O and 5H0I) with an r.m.s.d. value of 1.0 and 0.7 Å over 262 and 267 carbon alpha residues, respectively (Holm and Rosenström, 2010; Yang et al., 2017) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and supported by citations.

claim: Due to topological conservation, subtle differences around the substrate binding pocket will define substrate specificity and catalytic efficiency.
source: Due to such topological conservation it is expected that subtle differences around the substrate binding pocket will define substrate specificity and catalytic efficiency.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: HaAEP1 exhibits a unique flexible extension in the α5-β6 loop.
source: Indeed, comparison of these three structures reveals HaAEP1 exhibits a unique flexible extension, reflected by weak electron density, in the α5-β6 loop and differences between the residues that are local to the catalytic His and Cys and those that delineate the S3-S5 pockets (following the protease nomenclature defined by Schechter and Berger where the cleavage site residue is termed P1 and residues prior to and following the cleavage site are labeled P5-P2 and P1′-P2′, respectively, and where the corresponding binding sites on the protease are described as S5-S2′) (Schechter and Berger, 1967).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: HaAEP1 exhibits differences between the residues that are local to the catalytic His and Cys and those that delineate the S3-S5 pockets.
source: Indeed, comparison of these three structures reveals HaAEP1 exhibits a unique flexible extension, reflected by weak electron density, in the α5-β6 loop and differences between the residues that are local to the catalytic His and Cys and those that delineate the S3-S5 pockets (following the protease nomenclature defined by Schechter and Berger where the cleavage site residue is termed P1 and residues prior to and following the cleavage site are labeled P5-P2 and P1′-P2′, respectively, and where the corresponding binding sites on the protease are described as S5-S2′) (Schechter and Berger, 1967).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Differences in the substrate pocket include residues YGT 249–251 in HaAEP1 (hAEP: YAC 217–219, OaAEP1: WCY 246–248).
source: Specifically, differences in the substrate pocket include residues YGT 249–251 in HaAEP1 (hAEP: YAC 217–219, OaAEP1: WCY 246–248), a bulky Trp232 in hAEP versus Leu271 in HaAEP1 and Leu268 in OaAEP1, and the presence of an additional proline prior to the βIV-βV polyproline loop which orients E257 away from the S4 region in HaAEP1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: hAEP has a bulky Trp232 versus Leu271 in HaAEP1 and Leu268 in OaAEP1.
source: Specifically, differences in the substrate pocket include residues YGT 249–251 in HaAEP1 (hAEP: YAC 217–219, OaAEP1: WCY 246–248), a bulky Trp232 in hAEP versus Leu271 in HaAEP1 and Leu268 in OaAEP1, and the presence of an additional proline prior to the βIV-βV polyproline loop which orients E257 away from the S4 region in HaAEP1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: HaAEP1 has an additional proline prior to the βIV-βV polyproline loop which orients E257 away from the S4 region.
source: Specifically, differences in the substrate pocket include residues YGT 249–251 in HaAEP1 (hAEP: YAC 217–219, OaAEP1: WCY 246–248), a bulky Trp232 in hAEP versus Leu271 in HaAEP1 and Leu268 in OaAEP1, and the presence of an additional proline prior to the βIV-βV polyproline loop which orients E257 away from the S4 region in HaAEP1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: In OaAEP1, the C247 residue at the entrance to the S4 pocket was recently proposed to function as a 'gate keeper for ligation' with large bulky side chains inhibiting ligation.
source: In OaAEP1, the C247 residue at the entrance to the S4 pocket was recently proposed to function as a 'gate keeper for ligation' with large bulky side chains inhibiting ligation (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a proposal from the literature supported by citation.

claim: Differences local to the active site include residues P181, Q245, N247 in the βI sheet and β5-βIV loop (OaAEP1: A178, T242, S244, hAEP: T151, R213, S215).
source: Differences local to the active site include residues P181, Q245, N247 in the βI sheet and β5-βIV loop (OaAEP1: A178, T242, S244, hAEP: T151, R213, S215) and G185, E189, H191 in the βII-βIII region (OaAEP1: G182, K186, Y188, hAEP: V155, N158, D160) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Differences local to the active site include residues G185, E189, H191 in the βII-βIII region (OaAEP1: G182, K186, Y188, hAEP: V155, N158, D160).
source: Differences local to the active site include residues P181, Q245, N247 in the βI sheet and β5-βIV loop (OaAEP1: A178, T242, S244, hAEP: T151, R213, S215) and G185, E189, H191 in the βII-βIII region (OaAEP1: G182, K186, Y188, hAEP: V155, N158, D160) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: A 6-residue insertion in the α5-β6 loop results in the disruption of a potential N-linked glycosylation site that was hypothesized to affect substrate binding upstream to P5 in hAEP.
source: A 6-residue insertion in the α5-β6 loop results in the disruption of a potential N-linked glycosylation site that was hypothesized to affect substrate binding upstream to P5 in hAEP (Dall and Brandstetter, 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and supported by citation.

claim: None of the four conserved potential N-linked glycosylation sites in hAEP and mouse AEP (mAEP) are found in HaAEP1.
source: Interestingly, none of the four conserved potential N-linked glycosylation sites in hAEP and mouse AEP (mAEP) are found in HaAEP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: The only two potential N-linked glycosylation sites in HaAEP1 (N138 and N143) are located on the opposite side of the protein to the activation peptide in mammalian AEPs, at the beginning and center of the α2 helix, respectively.
source: Given that these glycosylation sites have been predicted to protect AEP from non-specific protease activation it is intriguing to find that the only two potential N-linked glycosylation sites in HaAEP1 (N138 and N143) are located on the opposite side of the protein to the activation peptide in mammalian AEPs, at the beginning and center of the α2 helix, respectively (Dall and Brandstetter, 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and supported by citation.

claim: Only N138 is prominently surface exposed in HaAEP1, suggesting that N-linked glycosylation in HaAEP1 is not utilized for mitigation against non-specific premature activation.
source: Moreover, only N138 is prominently surface exposed, suggesting that N-linked glycosylation in HaAEP1 is not utilized for mitigation against non-specific premature activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The 1.8 Å resolution of the HaAEP1 structure allowed observation of a succinimide moiety (Snn) below the catalytic His in a location identical to human AEP.
source: The 1.8 Å resolution of our HaAEP1 structure allowed us to observe a succinimide moiety (Snn) below the catalytic His in a location identical to human AEP (Figure 3A) that was hypothesized to play a role in peptide ligation (Dall et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on structural observation and supported by citation.

claim: The succinimide moiety was hypothesized to play a role in peptide ligation.
source: The 1.8 Å resolution of our HaAEP1 structure allowed us to observe a succinimide moiety (Snn) below the catalytic His in a location identical to human AEP (Figure 3A) that was hypothesized to play a role in peptide ligation (Dall et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citation.

claim: Dual conformations of the catalytic His178 and Cys220 residues were distinguished, which are hypothesized to represent conformational changes that occur during catalysis and correspond to substrate free and reaction intermediate states.
source: We distinguished dual conformations of the catalytic His178 and Cys220 residues which we hypothesize represent conformational changes that occur during catalysis and correspond to substrate free and reaction intermediate states (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on structural observation and is a hypothesis.

claim: In the intermediate state the catalytic Cys Sδ is oriented ~95° towards the Nδ of the catalytic His imidazole ring which is orientated ~3.8 Å closer to this residue in the corresponding intermediate state.

claim: A pH-dependent activity has been well documented for cysteine proteases and is a function of the formation of a thiolate and imidazolium ions on the catalytic dyad of Cys and His residues.
